intro:
Every analysis in this study, in reading order. Each entry says what we
wanted to know, what we did, how we tested it, what came out, and what
followed from it.

Every technical term used below, such as AP, AUROC, held-out, bootstrap or
tier, is explained in plain language in `docs/GLOSSARY.md`, which also
explains how to read each figure.

phases.title: Data and cohorts
phases.intro:
Who the study is about, what is predicted, and how every result is tested
fairly.

entries.title: The outcome and the cohort
entries.question: What exactly is predicted, and for whom?
entries.did:
- Took the 2024-25 Ethiopia DHS women's file and kept the **6,893 women**
  whose most recent pregnancy has a recorded number of antenatal contacts.
- Defined three nested outcomes on that count: ANC1+, ANC4+ and ANC8+.
entries.tested:
The code asserts, woman by woman, that ANC8+ implies
ANC4+ implies ANC1+. All figures are survey-weighted.
entries.found:
77.6% of women reach ANC1+, 52.4% ANC4+ and 19.2%
ANC8+. The biggest loss is between the fourth and eighth contacts: only 37%
of women who reach four go on to eight.
entries.changed:
ANC8+ is the main outcome; ANC1+ and ANC4+ are studied as
the earlier rungs of the same ladder.

entries.title: One held-out set, for everything
entries.question: How do we test a model fairly?
entries.did:
Split the women once, by survey cluster within stratum
(seed 2026):
- **5,518 for development**, to build, compare and tune;
- **1,375 held out**, scored only at the end.

The same split, restricted to their women, serves the ANC-entry cohort
(4,017 / 984) and the 24-month window (4,040 / 997).
entries.tested:
The test suite checks that no cluster spans two folds,
and that the ANC-entry partition matches the full split woman for woman.
entries.found:
The held-out set contains only 229 women who
reached ANC8+, so comparisons on it carry wide uncertainty.
entries.changed:
Every result in the study is scored on these same women,
and every held-out comparison carries a paired bootstrap interval.

entries.title: Checked against the official report
entries.question: Is the outcome defined the way the official survey defines it?
entries.did:
- Read the *Guide to DHS Statistics* (DHS-8) and the 2024-25 EDHS key
  indicators report.
- Recomputed the report's regional ANC4+ table on its own 24-month window,
  with pregnancy timing taken from the pregnancy history so that stillbirths
  are kept.
entries.tested: Our figure against the report's, region by region.
entries.found:
National ANC4+ **53.0% against 53.0%**; 13 of 14 regions
within 0.8 points.
entries.changed:
This validates the outcome, weights and region coding. The
24-month window (5,037 women) is kept as a sensitivity check on every result.

phases.title: The candidate pool
phases.intro:
Before asking which predictors matter, decide which could legitimately be
predictors at all.

entries.title: Screening every survey column
entries.question:
Which of the survey's 6,648 columns could predict antenatal
care?
entries.did:
- Excluded, automatically, columns not collected in this round (1,719),
  entirely missing (808), measured at or after the delivery (2,296), observed
  for under half the cohort (1,208) or administrative (28).
- Scored the remaining **577** on their own, on development women only, and
  reviewed each for timing and relevance.
entries.tested:
The screening was rerun on development women alone and
compared with the whole-cohort run.
entries.found:
- **61 survey variables admitted**; 507 not admitted, with a median
  univariate AUC of 0.518 (almost no signal), mostly from post-birth modules.
- The strongest legitimate predictor is the **continuous wealth score**
  (univariate AUC 0.755).
- All 61 survive development-only screening; the largest AUC shift is 0.013.
entries.changed:
A full candidate pool of 95 columns: the 61, the 21-set
constructs and derived measures such as log travel times and separate media
channels.

entries.title: Refusing the variables that record the care itself
entries.question: Which strong candidates must not be used?
entries.did:
Checked the strongest candidates against when they were
measured.
entries.tested:
For "visited a health facility in the last 12
months", compared attenders and non-attenders by how recent the birth was.
entries.found:
Among women whose birth was within 12 months, 67% of ANC
attenders report a facility visit against 28% of non-attenders, a gap that
narrows once the birth falls outside the recall window: the outcome being
re-reported. HIV testing, contraception at interview and first-contact
timing are refused for the same reason.
entries.changed:
Nine strong candidates refused with written reasons;
first-contact timing admitted only at the ANC-entry horizon.

entries.title: Merging copies of the same variable
entries.question: Is any variable in the pool twice?
entries.did:
Searched for pairs carrying the same information, using
Theil's U in both directions, which separates true copies from structurally
missing categories (for example "not applicable" for unmarried women).
entries.tested:
Refitting without the copies, and restating importance
per variable.
entries.found:
**10 of the 95 columns are copies: 85 distinct
variables.** Removing them changes AP by 0.002, but importance had been split
between copies: travel time to hospital rises from rank 10 to rank 2 once its
copy is counted.
entries.changed:
The predictor-value study uses 88 candidates: the 85 plus
the three constructs only the 21-predictor set has. Importance is always
reported with copies merged.

phases.title: Predictor value
phases.intro:
The central analysis: which predictors carry the prediction of each rung,
and how many are needed.

entries.title: A fair way to compare predictor sets
entries.question:
How do we compare *variables* without the model or its
settings tipping the scales?
entries.did:
- **Fixed model:** logistic regression, scored on 5 repeated
  cluster-grouped splits of the development women.
- **Per-set regularisation** from a common grid, because a single setting
  favours small or large sets (the 88 score 0.478 at a light setting and 0.508
  at their own best).
- **The bar**, fixed before any selection result: a variable counts only if
  it changes AP by at least 0.005 on average and on 4 of 5 splits.
entries.tested:
The fast scorer against the full scikit-learn pipeline:
identical AP.
entries.found: Nothing yet; this entry is about the method.
entries.changed: Every predictor comparison below uses this setup.

entries.title: Dropping each of the 21
entries.question:
Does every member of the 21-predictor set earn its place, at
each rung?
entries.did:
Removed each of the 21 in turn and rescored the rest, for
ANC1+, ANC4+ and ANC8+.
entries.tested: AP lost on each of 5 splits.
entries.found:
- Region, pregnancy intention and wealth carry the 21 at every rung.
- Members that add nothing: **8 of 21 for ANC1+, 10 for ANC4+, 14 for
  ANC8+**. Health insurance, household size, religion, the weekly media count,
  internet use and transport mode add nothing to any rung.
entries.changed: Motivated the question of how many of the 21 are needed.

entries.title: How many of the 21 are needed
entries.question:
What is the smallest subset of the 21 that does as well as all
21?
entries.did:
Greedy forward selection within the 21, run all the way to
21, and the 21 without all its non-contributors at once.
entries.tested:
Development AP as a share of the full pool's lift over
prevalence.
entries.found:
- **ANC8+:** the path peaks at **7 predictors**, reaching the full pool's
  development AP (0.509), and every further member lowers it; all 21 reach
  0.469.
- **ANC1+ and ANC4+:** the path is flat after about 8-11 predictors; the 21
  are about as good as their best subset.
entries.changed:
The reduced sets were taken to the held-out test, because
they were chosen on the same folds they were scored on.

entries.title: What the rest of the pool adds
entries.question: Of the 67 pool candidates outside the 21, how many add value?
entries.tested:
Development AP, gain on each of 5 splits, the +0.005
bar.
entries.found:
- **ANC1+ and ANC4+:** none clears the bar alone.
- **ANC8+:** 8 of 67 do; the wealth score gains most (+0.017).
- Stacking on ANC8+: the best 5 carry 88% of the gain.
entries.changed:
Individually, almost none of the 67 matter; the collective
value is judged on held-out women.

entries.title: Building from nothing: the tiers
entries.question: Starting from zero, which variables would the data choose?
entries.did:
- Forward selection over all 88, stopping at the first step that fails the
  bar. Tier 1 runs to 90% of the full pool's lift; tier 2 is the rest that
  pass.
- For ANC8+, the selection repeated on 10 bootstrap resamples.
entries.tested:
Gain per step on 5 splits, and how often each variable
was chosen again.
entries.found:
- The **wealth score is chosen first in every run** and **region** in every
  run; **pregnancy intention** enters for ANC4+ and ANC8+ but not ANC1+.
- Sets of **2 (ANC1+), 4 (ANC4+) and 8 (ANC8+)** predictors.
- Stability for ANC8+: wealth 100%, intention 90%, region 80%, health-post
  access 60%; most other places rotate.
entries.changed: The compact candidate sets for the held-out test.

entries.title: Every set, on the held-out women
entries.question:
Which number of predictors holds up on women who played no
part in choosing it?
entries.did:
Fitted every set on development women and scored it once on
the held-out women: tier 1, tier 1+2, the best k of the 21, the 21 without
its non-contributors, all 21 and the full pool, with paired bootstrap
intervals against the 21. The tiers were also refitted with LightGBM.
entries.tested:
Held-out AP and AUROC, paired stratified-PSU
bootstrap.
entries.found:
- **ANC8+:** 7 of the 21 (0.440), the 8 selected from the pool (0.425), all
  21 (0.428) and the full pool (0.435) cannot be separated: every interval
  includes zero. **7 to 8 predictors are enough.**
- **ANC4+ and ANC1+:** the full pool beats the 21 (+0.023 and +0.014 AP,
  intervals excluding zero); compact sets fall slightly short.
entries.changed:
The selection result is stated per rung: a short set for
completing care, the full pool for reaching it.

phases.title: Across the ladder
phases.intro:
The same women, predictors and folds at three rungs: what changes from
reaching care to completing it.

entries.title: How predictable each rung is
entries.question: Is completing care harder to predict than reaching it?
entries.did:
Built ten model families for ANC1+, ANC4+ and ANC8+ on the
full pool, and scored each rung's development champion on held-out women.
entries.tested:
Held-out AUROC and lift, because raw AP cannot be
compared across outcomes with different prevalences.
entries.found:
AUROC falls **0.83 → 0.79 → 0.76** from ANC1+ to ANC8+.
Completing care is genuinely harder to predict.
entries.changed:
Every cross-rung comparison uses AUROC, lift, or a share of
each rung's ceiling.

entries.title: Each predictor's value at each rung
entries.question: Which predictors gain or lose value from ANC1+ to ANC8+?
entries.did:
Put every predictor's marginal value relative to the 21 (AP
lost when dropped, or gained when added) on one scale: a share of each rung's
ceiling above prevalence.
entries.tested: The same development splits for all three rungs.
entries.found:
- **Region** is worth 2.7% of the ANC1+ ceiling and 8.7% of the ANC8+
  ceiling; the **wealth score** 0.3% and 5.4%.
- Say in large purchases, water source and living at a health post matter
  only for completing the schedule.
- Residence, the gap since the previous pregnancy and sex of the household
  head matter only for reaching care.
entries.changed:
The ladder finding stated per predictor, not only by
domain.

entries.title: Importance, three ways
entries.question: Do independent importance methods show the same shift?
entries.did:
Measured each predictor's importance at each rung with
exact EBM contributions, SHAP on XGBoost and drop-one, normalised to a share
within the rung, with copies merged. A pattern counts only if two methods
agree. SHAP uses XGBoost at every rung because its tree explainer mishandles
HistGradientBoosting's categorical splits.
entries.tested: Rank agreement between methods.
entries.found:
- Agency and household factors carry the most for reaching care (28%) and
  the least for completing it (19%); socioeconomic factors (20% → 26%),
  pregnancy intention and access rise.
- EBM and SHAP agree well (0.58 to 0.76); drop-one agrees weakly.
entries.changed:
Household position gets women through the door; money,
distance and wanting the pregnancy keep them coming back.

phases.title: Two prediction horizons
phases.intro:
Before ANC starts, and at ANC entry, when the timing of the first contact is
known.

entries.title: The ANC-entry cohort
entries.question: Who can be predicted at ANC entry, and on which split?
entries.tested:
The code asserts that the entry partition matches the
full split woman for woman (4,017 / 984).
entries.found:
Every woman at this horizon has ANC1+, so only ANC4+ and
ANC8+ are predicted.
entries.changed:
The whole predictor-value study was repeated at this
horizon, with early ANC as an 89th candidate.

entries.title: What early initiation adds
entries.question: How much does knowing that the first contact was early add?
entries.did:
Added early ANC to the 21, to the entry selected set and to
the full pool; ran forward selection and bootstrap re-selection at entry; and
scored every set once on the 984 held-out entry women.
entries.tested:
Development gain on 5 splits, then paired bootstrap on
held-out women.
entries.found:
- Early ANC is the strongest single addition at both rungs (+0.032 AP for
  ANC4+, +0.077 for ANC8+) and is selected second, after the wealth score;
  for ANC8+ in 10 of 10 resamples.
- **ANC4+:** wealth score and early ANC (2 predictors) beat all 21 on
  held-out women (AP 0.880 against 0.848, interval excluding zero).
- **ANC8+:** about 7 predictors; early ANC's held-out gain over the 21
  (+0.027 AP) cannot be confirmed on 984 women.
entries.changed:
At ANC entry the recommended set is 2-3 predictors for
ANC4+ and about 7 for ANC8+, each led by wealth and early initiation.

entries.title: One model or two
entries.question:
Is a model fitted on the ANC-entry women better for them than
one fitted on everyone?
entries.did:
Fitted the 21 and the full pool on all development women and
on the entry development women, and scored both on the same held-out entry
women, without early ANC.
entries.tested: Paired bootstrap of the AUROC difference.
entries.found:
No measurable difference (+0.004 to +0.014 AUROC, every
interval including zero).
entries.changed:
What matters at entry is adding the timing of the first
contact, not refitting on the entry population.

phases.title: The Tigray war
phases.intro:
Pregnancies during and after the war, against every other region. The survey
records ANC only for births from about mid-2021, so no pre-war pregnancy is
observed.

entries.title: Wartime against post-war, net of other regions
entries.question: What did the war do to antenatal care in Tigray?
entries.did:
- A pregnancy is "wartime" if at least 3 of its 9 months fell inside the war
  (3 Nov 2020 – 2 Nov 2022, cited in `docs/conflict_windows.csv`), and
  "post-war" if conceived after the ceasefire.
- Difference-in-differences against regions without major conflict, with the
  comparison change averaged **within** each region (pooling produces a
  spurious 5-point fall, a Simpson's paradox).
entries.tested:
Stratified cluster bootstrap; the war window shifted
±3 months; Oromia and Benishangul-Gumuz added to the comparison group.
entries.found:
Tigray wartime pregnancies (n = 259) against post-war
(n = 323):
- **no ANC at all: 19.5% → 7.7%**, 13 points beyond other regions
  [−20.3, −6.2];
- ANC4+ +13.6 points; ANC8+ no clear change (+2.0).

The ANC4+ result stays between +11 and +14 under every robustness check.
entries.changed:
The war's damage was at the door: access recovered,
completion did not.

entries.title: Tigray against every region
entries.question:
How does Tigray's change compare with every other region over
the same calendar periods?
entries.did:
Computed ANC levels in every region for pregnancies in the
war window and pregnancies conceived after the ceasefire.
entries.tested: Survey-weighted levels, region by region.
entries.found:
Tigray's change in reaching care is the largest of any
region (no-ANC −12 points, ANC4+ +14); most regions move a few points. Its
ANC8+ barely moves.
entries.changed:
The difference-in-differences is shown against the levels
behind it.

entries.title: Tigray against its own circumstances
entries.question:
Tigray sits about 4 points below expectation on ANC8+. Is that
only the war?
entries.did:
Compared each region's attainment with what its population
profile predicts (region withheld), on all births, on post-war pregnancies
only, and in the 24-month window.
entries.tested: The same model in each cohort.
entries.found:
Post-war, Tigray is **above** expectation for reaching
care (ANC1+ +6.3, ANC4+ +7.4 points) and still **below** it for completing
care (ANC8+ −2.8). The regional ranking is stable across windows.
entries.changed: Tigray's completion shortfall is not only a war artefact.

phases.title: Supporting analyses
phases.intro:
Could the results be an artefact of the modelling? Each of these asks one
version of that question.

entries.title: Ten model families, tuned on the same folds
entries.question: With the full pool, does the choice of algorithm matter?
entries.did:
Tuned ten families with Optuna on identical folds and the
same objective (weighted AP), choosing the champion on development folds.
entries.tested: Development out-of-fold AP, then held-out AP.
entries.found:
Development AP ranged only from 0.501 to 0.518; every
model dropped about **0.08 AP** on held-out women, more than the gap between
models.
entries.changed: The algorithm is not the constraint; the predictors are.

entries.title: Calibration, and an additive model
entries.question: Can the predicted probabilities be read as honest rates?
entries.did: Added Platt or isotonic calibration, fitted on inner folds.
entries.tested: Calibration slope and AP cost.
entries.found:
- Platt moved the slope from 0.62 to **0.99** at a cost of 0.005 AP;
  isotonic cost 0.023.
- The Explainable Boosting Machine, offered ten interactions, **chose none**
  and matched XGBoost on AUROC (0.789 against 0.788): ANC8+ attainment
  behaves additively.
entries.changed:
The EBM is the model the app explains, with exact
per-predictor contributions.

entries.title: Modelling the whole count
entries.question: Does modelling the contact count, not just "8 or more", help?
entries.did:
A cumulative-link model of the count, reading off "at least
8".
entries.tested:
Development and held-out AP against the plain yes/no
model.
entries.found:
Better in development (0.500 against 0.494), **worse on
held-out women (0.402 against 0.427)**.
entries.changed: Reported, not used.

entries.title: What tuning and preprocessing bought
entries.question:
How much of the accuracy comes from tuning and data
preparation?
entries.did:
Refitted each tuned model at library defaults, moved each
setting one step with the others fixed, and tried four preprocessing
variants with everything else fixed.
entries.tested: Development AP against the tuned optimum.
entries.found:
Tuning bought +0.02 to +0.04 AP, less than the 0.08
optimism gap; preprocessing at most +0.003.
entries.changed: Neither is a lever; the choice of predictors is.

entries.title: The full pool against the 21, on repeated splits
entries.question:
Is the difference between the full pool and the 21 real, on
evidence that would convince a sceptic?
entries.did:
20 fresh random splits of all women, each refit from
scratch with the model fixed and only the predictors changed; and a paired
bootstrap on the held-out women.
entries.tested: AP differences with 95% intervals, and splits won.
entries.found:
- Repeated splits: **+0.031 AP, better in 20 of 20**.
- Held-out: +0.021 AP [−0.036, +0.075]; one set of 1,375 women cannot
  resolve a gain this size.
- Within most regions the models rank women much less well than nationally.
entries.changed:
Set comparisons rest on repeated splits, with the held-out
interval always reported next to them.

entries.title: The 24-month window
entries.question: Do the predictor results hold on the official 24-month window?
entries.did:
Repeated the predictor-value study on the 5,037 women with a
birth in the last 24 months.
entries.tested: The same stages and held-out test.
entries.found:
The same leaders: the wealth score first in every run,
region in every run, pregnancy intention for ANC4+ and ANC8+; years of
schooling also enters.
entries.changed: The main results do not depend on including older births.

glossary.start:
Imagine 100 women who gave birth recently. **19 of them completed eight or
more antenatal care contacts (ANC8+)** and 81 did not. That is close to the
real national figure of 19.2%.

A model looks at facts about each woman (her household's wealth, her region,
whether she wanted the pregnancy, and so on) and gives her a score between 0
and 1: its estimate of how likely she is to reach eight contacts.

**Why we don't report "accuracy".** Accuracy is the share of women the model
labels correctly. A "model" that ignores every fact and says *no woman will
reach eight contacts* is right about the 81 who did not. Its accuracy is 81%,
and it is completely useless. When one outcome is much rarer than the other,
accuracy rewards ignoring the rare one. So this analysis uses measures that
cannot be gamed this way.

**Ranking, not labelling.** Sort the 100 women from highest score to lowest.
A good model puts most of the 19 near the top. Every measure below is a way
of asking *how near the top?*

**Precision and recall.** Suppose a programme can visit the 20 women with the
highest scores. If 10 of those 20 actually reached eight contacts:

- **precision** is 10 out of 20 = 50%: of the women we picked, how many were
  right;
- **recall** is 10 out of 19 = 53%: of all the women who really reached eight
  contacts, how many we found.

Visiting more women raises recall and usually lowers precision.

**Average precision (AP).** Walk down the sorted list and record the
precision each time you reach another woman who really attained the outcome.
AP is the average of those precisions. It is 1.0 if all 19 are at the very
top. If the model ranks at random, AP is about **0.19**: the share of women
who attain the outcome, because a random pick is right 19% of the time. So:

> **AP always has to be read against the prevalence.** An AP of 0.43 on
> ANC8+ (prevalence 0.19) is a real signal. An AP of 0.43 on ANC1+
> (prevalence 0.78) would be worse than guessing.

**AUROC (also written AUC).** Pick one woman who reached eight contacts and
one who did not, at random. AUROC is the chance that the model gave the first
woman the higher score. A coin flip gives **0.5**, perfect ranking gives
**1.0**. Our models score about **0.76 to 0.83**: they put the right woman of
the pair higher about three times in four. AUROC does not depend on how
common the outcome is. That is why it is the measure used to compare ANC1+,
ANC4+ and ANC8+ with each other.

**Lift.** AP minus the prevalence: how much better than a blind guess. On
ANC8+, AP 0.427 minus 0.192 = lift **+0.236**.

**Calibration.** Take all the women the model gave a score of about 30%. If
about 30 in 100 of them really reached eight contacts, the model is **well
calibrated**: its scores can be read as rates. A model can rank well and
still be badly calibrated, for example by saying 60% where the true rate is
40%.

**The size of differences in this analysis.** Most comparisons here are
changes in AP of **0.005 to 0.04**, which is half a point to four points out
of 100. When one set of predictors "adds +0.03 AP", the model's ranking of
women improved by about three points on that 0-to-1 scale.

terms.name: Antenatal care (ANC)
terms.plain:
Health checks during pregnancy with a doctor, nurse,
midwife or health officer. Each check is a "contact".
terms.here:
The number of contacts a woman reported for her most
recent pregnancy, taken from the survey.

terms.name: ANC1+, ANC4+ and ANC8+
terms.here:
Nationally 77.6%, 52.4% and 19.2% of women reach each
level (survey-weighted, all 6,893 women). We call the three levels the
"ladder", and each level a "rung".

terms.name: Cascade
terms.plain:
The ladder read as a sequence of losses: women who never
start, who start but stop before four, who reach four but stop before eight,
and who reach eight.
terms.here:
Counted directly from the survey, with no model
involved. This makes it the sturdiest evidence in the analysis.

terms.name: Continuation
terms.plain:
Of the women who reached one rung, the share who went on
to the next.
terms.here:
68% of women who start go on to four contacts. Only
37% of those who reach four go on to eight.

terms.name: Prevalence
terms.plain:
How common the outcome is: the share of women who
attained it.
terms.here:
0.776 for ANC1+, 0.524 for ANC4+ and 0.192 for ANC8+.
It is also the AP a model with no information would get, so it is the floor
every AP must be read against.

terms.name: DHS (Demographic and Health Survey)
terms.plain:
A large national household survey, run in many countries
with the same questions, so results can be compared.
terms.here:
The 2024-25 Ethiopia DHS women's file (the
"Individual Recode"). It has 6,648 columns, one row per woman interviewed.

terms.name: Cohort
terms.plain: The group of women an analysis is about.
terms.here:
Three groups:
- the **6,893 women** whose most recent pregnancy has a recorded ANC count
  (the main analysis, and the first prediction horizon);
- the **5,001 women** among them who started ANC and know when their first
  contact was (the second prediction horizon);
- the **5,037 women** who gave birth in the 24 months before interview (a
  sensitivity check).

terms.name: 24-month window
terms.plain:
The official survey definition only counts births in the
two years before the interview. Older births are recalled less reliably.
terms.here:
5,037 women. With this window, our numbers reproduce
the official EDHS report's national ANC4+ figure exactly (53.0% against
53.0%). About 28% of the 6,893 women gave birth 2-3 years before
interview. Used as a sensitivity check on the main results.

terms.name: Survey weight
terms.plain:
The survey deliberately samples some areas more heavily
than others. Each woman carries a weight so that the results represent the
whole country, not just the sample.
terms.here: Every percentage and every accuracy score is weighted.

terms.name: Cluster (PSU)
terms.plain:
The survey visits small areas (villages or city blocks)
and interviews several women in each. Women in the same area resemble each
other.
terms.here:
A cluster is never split between training and testing.
If it were, the model would be tested partly on the neighbours of women it
learned from, which flatters it.

terms.name: Stratum
terms.plain:
The survey divides the country into groups (region ×
urban/rural) and samples inside each group separately.
terms.here:
There are 27 strata. Test sets and bootstrap resamples
keep every stratum represented.

terms.name: Predictor
terms.plain:
One fact about a woman that the model uses: her region,
her household's wealth, whether she wanted the pregnancy, and so on.
terms.here:
Two sets are compared throughout. The
**21-predictor set** is the study's pre-specified set of constructs across
four domains. The **full candidate pool** comes from screening all 6,648
survey columns: 95 columns, which are 85 distinct variables because 10 were
copies of each other. The predictor-value study uses 88: the 85 plus 3
constructs that exist only in the 21-predictor set.

terms.name: Temporality
terms.plain:
A predictor must describe something known *before or
early in* the pregnancy. Otherwise the model would be "predicting" care from
facts that come after it.
terms.here:
Predictors measured at interview (for example "worked
in the last year") are marked ⚑. They may partly describe life after the
birth.

terms.name: Leakage
terms.plain:
A predictor that secretly contains the answer. For
example, "visited a health facility in the last 12 months" is partly the ANC
visits themselves. A model using it looks excellent and is useless.

terms.name: Development set and held-out set
terms.plain:
The women are split once:
- the **development set** (5,518 women) is used to build, compare and tune
  models;
- the **held-out set** (1,375 women) is locked away and used only at the
  end, to see how a finished model does on women it has never seen.

This is the only fair test.
terms.here:
One split, drawn once by survey cluster and used for
every analysis, outcome and horizon, so every result is scored on the same
women. The held-out set has only 229 women who reached ANC8+, so its
verdicts come with wide uncertainty. At the ANC-entry horizon the split is
the same one, restricted to the 5,001 women who started ANC (4,017
development, 984 held out).

terms.name: Cross-validation and folds
terms.plain:
A way to test inside the development set without
touching the held-out women:
1. cut the development women into 5 groups ("folds");
2. train on 4 of them and score the 5th;
3. repeat until every group has been scored once.

The resulting "out-of-fold" score uses every development woman exactly once
as a test case.
terms.here:
Folds are cut by cluster and balanced by stratum.
"Development AP" always means this out-of-fold AP.

terms.name: Repeated splits and seeds
terms.plain:
One split into groups can be lucky or unlucky, so the
whole comparison is repeated with different random splits. The "seed" is the
number that fixes one random split, so it can be reproduced exactly.
terms.here:
"Better in 20 of 20 splits" means the comparison was
run on 20 different random splits and one side won every time. That is
strong evidence even when each individual gain is small.

terms.name: Overfitting and optimism
terms.plain:
A model or a choice fitted too closely to the data it was
built on does better there than on new data. Any choice made by comparing
scores on the same folds (which model, which settings, which predictors)
makes those folds' scores optimistic.
terms.here:
Every model's development AP ran about **0.08 higher**
than its held-out AP. So a development gain smaller than 0.08 is not, on its
own, proof of a better model.

terms.name: Champion
terms.plain: The model chosen as the best.
terms.here:
The champion is always chosen on **development**
scores and only then scored on held-out women. Choosing it by the held-out
score would make that score optimistic. That mistake was made once and
corrected.

terms.name: Paired comparison
terms.plain:
Two models scored on exactly the same women, so the
difference reflects the models and not which women happened to be tested.
terms.here: Every "A vs B" difference is paired.

terms.name: Accuracy
terms.plain: The share of women labelled correctly.
terms.here:
Not used. With 19% prevalence, labelling everyone "no"
scores 81% (see "Start here").

terms.name: Precision and recall
terms.plain:
- **Precision:** of the women the model flags, the share who really attain
  the outcome.
- **Recall** (also called sensitivity): of the women who really attain it,
  the share the model flags.
- **Specificity** is recall for the other group.
terms.here:
They depend on where you draw the line (the
threshold), so they are reported only at stated thresholds. AP summarises
them across all thresholds.

terms.name: Average precision (AP)
terms.plain:
How well the model packs the women who attain the
outcome at the top of its ranking, averaged over the whole list. It runs
from the prevalence (random) to 1.0 (perfect).
terms.here:
The headline measure *within* one outcome, because it
focuses on the rarer group. Never compare raw AP across ANC1+, ANC4+ and
ANC8+: their floors are 0.78, 0.52 and 0.19.
terms.good:
Clearly above the prevalence. On ANC8+ the
models reach 0.40 to 0.46 on held-out women, against a floor of 0.19.

terms.name: AUROC (AUC)
terms.plain:
Take one woman who attained the outcome and one who did
not. AUROC is the chance the model scored the first one higher. 0.5 is a
coin flip, 1.0 is perfect.
terms.here:
The measure used to compare rungs, because it ignores
prevalence. The champions score 0.826 (ANC1+), 0.789 (ANC4+) and 0.759
(ANC8+) on held-out women: completing care is harder to predict than
reaching it.
terms.good:
0.7 to 0.8 is typical and useful for
population health. Above 0.9 is rare for survey data, and suspicious if seen
(check for leakage).

terms.name: Lift
terms.plain:
AP minus the prevalence: the improvement over a blind
guess. "Share of possible lift" divides it by the most it could be
(1 − prevalence).
terms.here: Used alongside AUROC for fair cross-rung comparisons.

terms.name: Univariate AUC
terms.plain:
The AUROC of one variable on its own: how well that
single fact ranks women.
terms.here:
The continuous wealth score alone reaches 0.755,
nearly as high as the whole 21-predictor XGBoost model (0.761).

terms.name: Calibration
terms.plain:
Whether the scores can be read as rates. Among women
given 30%, do about 30% attain the outcome?
terms.here:
Checked on held-out women. A calibration map (Platt
scaling) was added because the raw scores were too extreme.

terms.name: Calibration slope
terms.plain:
- **Slope 1.0** is ideal.
- **Below 1** means the scores are too spread out: too confident at both
  ends, the usual sign of overfitting.
- **Above 1** means they are too timid.

"Calibration-in-the-large" (CITL) asks whether the average score matches the
average outcome. 0 is ideal.
terms.here:
The 21-predictor models had slopes of 0.78 to 0.86.
After Platt scaling the full-pool model's slope is 0.99.

terms.name: Brier score
terms.plain:
The average squared gap between the score and what
happened (1 or 0). Lower is better. It rewards both ranking and calibration.
terms.here:
Reported in the tables, for example 0.113 for the
21-predictor XGBoost. It is not a headline measure.

terms.name: Net benefit and decision curves
terms.plain:
Would using the model to decide whom to act on beat the
simple alternatives of acting on everyone or on no one? Net benefit counts
correct actions and subtracts wrong ones, weighted by how costly a wrong
action is judged to be (the threshold).
terms.here:
The models beat both defaults across the useful range
of thresholds, but the 21-predictor and full-pool models are nearly
identical on this measure.

terms.name: Threshold (operating point)
terms.plain:
The score above which a woman is flagged. Changing it
trades precision against recall.
terms.here:
Thresholds were set on development data, never on
held-out women. "Risk bands" group women by their predicted probability.

terms.name: Bootstrap
terms.here:
Clusters are redrawn whole and each stratum is kept,
matching how the survey was designed. That makes the intervals honest rather
than too narrow.

terms.name: Confidence interval
terms.plain:
A range, written like [−0.036, +0.075], that the true
value very probably lies in. A narrow range means a precise estimate; a wide
range means we don't know the value well.
terms.here:
95% intervals from the bootstrap, written in square
brackets after the estimate.

terms.name: "The interval includes zero"
terms.plain:
If the range for a *difference* runs from negative to
positive, the data cannot tell whether A or B is really better. That is not
proof they are equal, only that this sample is too small to separate them.
terms.here:
The full-pool model's held-out advantage over the
21-predictor XGBoost (+0.021 AP) has an interval of [−0.036, +0.075], so this
held-out set alone cannot confirm it. The claim therefore rests on repeated
splits (20 of 20).

terms.name: Significance
terms.plain:
A shorthand for "the interval for the difference
excludes zero".
terms.here:
With the 21 predictors, XGBoost was *not*
significantly better than logistic regression on any measure.

terms.name: Logistic regression
terms.plain:
The classic statistical model. Each predictor adds or
subtracts a fixed amount from a woman's log-odds (see "Log-odds"), and the
total becomes a probability. "Regularisation" shrinks the effects so the
model doesn't chase noise. Its strength is called C.
terms.here:
Used as the fixed model when comparing predictor sets,
because it has almost nothing to tune and so cannot favour one set through
its settings.

terms.name: Tree ensembles
terms.plain:
Models built from hundreds of simple yes/no decision
trees:
- **random forest** and **extra trees** average many trees grown
  independently;
- **gradient boosting** (XGBoost, LightGBM, HistGradientBoosting, CatBoost)
  grows trees one after another, each correcting the previous ones.

They capture interactions automatically.
terms.here:
All were tried. None beat the others by a meaningful
margin: the spread across ten families was about 0.02 development AP.

terms.name: Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM)
terms.plain:
A model that learns one curve per predictor and adds
them up. Every prediction can be read exactly as the sum of its parts.
terms.here:
It matched the best tree ensemble on AUROC and is the
model behind the What-if tab. Offered up to ten interactions between
predictors, it chose none: ANC8+ attainment behaves additively.

terms.name: Neural network (MLP)
terms.plain:
Layers of simple arithmetic units trained together, the
same family as modern AI, here very small.
terms.here:
One of the ten families. It had the best held-out AP
on ANC8+ (0.463), but it was not the development champion. Picking it
because of its held-out score would be the selection mistake described under
"Champion".

terms.name: Ordinal (cumulative-link) model
terms.plain:
Instead of a yes/no outcome, it models the contact count
itself (at least 1, at least 2, ...) and reads off "at least 8".
terms.here:
Better in development (0.500 against 0.494 AP), worse
on held-out women (0.402 against 0.427). Reported, not used.

terms.name: Hyperparameters and tuning
terms.plain:
Settings chosen before training, such as how deep a tree
may grow or how strongly to regularise. **Tuning** tries many combinations
and keeps the best. **Optuna** is the tool that runs this search.
**Library defaults** are the settings a model ships with.
terms.here:
Tuning raised development AP by +0.02 to +0.04 over
library defaults. That is less than the 0.08 optimism gap, so it is not
evidence that tuned models generalise better.

terms.name: Platt scaling
terms.plain:
A small correction applied after the model, fitted on
separate data, that turns over- or under-confident scores into honest rates.
**Isotonic** is a more flexible alternative.
terms.here:
Platt raised the calibration slope from 0.62 to 0.99
at almost no cost in ranking (−0.005 AP). It is the calibration that ships.

terms.name: The 21-predictor set and the full pool
terms.plain:
The two predictor sets every comparison is built around.
- **The 21-predictor set:** 21 constructs chosen in advance from the
  literature, in four domains (maternal, household, pregnancy, access),
  modelled with logistic regression, random forest and XGBoost.
- **The full candidate pool:** everything that survived screening the whole
  survey file for timing and leakage, modelled with ten model families.
terms.here:
The question is not which set "wins" but which of their
members carry the prediction: how few are needed, which of the 21 add
nothing, and what the rest of the pool adds.

terms.name: Prediction horizon
terms.plain:
The moment a prediction is made, which decides what can
be known.
- **Before ANC starts:** only who the woman is, her household and where she
  lives.
- **At ANC entry:** the same, plus when her first contact happened.
terms.here:
The predictor-value study is run at both horizons. At
ANC entry every woman has at least one contact, so only ANC4+ and ANC8+ can
be predicted.

terms.name: Early ANC
terms.plain:
Whether the first antenatal contact came in the first
trimester (by 12 weeks or 3 months).
terms.here:
Admissible only at the ANC-entry horizon: before a
woman starts care it is not yet known, and using it there would be leakage.

terms.name: Feature importance
terms.plain:
How much the model relies on each predictor. It says
nothing about cause.
terms.here:
Measured three independent ways (EBM, SHAP and
drop-one). Each is turned into a share of the total within each rung, so the
rungs can be compared.

terms.name: Log-odds
terms.here: Importance and shape-function charts use this scale.

terms.name: SHAP
terms.plain:
A method that splits one prediction into
contributions from each predictor, borrowed from game theory ("how much did
each player contribute to the team's score?").
terms.here:
Computed on XGBoost for every rung. An earlier run
computed ANC4+ SHAP on a model type the method mishandles. That was caught
and corrected.

terms.name: Drop-one importance
terms.plain:
Refit the model without one predictor and see how much
AP falls. A negative value means the model is *better* without it.
terms.here:
Removing members of the 21 one at a time, 8 add
nothing for ANC1+, 10 for ANC4+ and 14 for ANC8+. Drop-one understates
predictors that have a close substitute, because the substitute compensates,
so it is treated as the weakest of the three importance methods.

terms.name: Shape function
terms.plain:
The EBM's learned curve for one predictor: how a
woman's score moves as that one fact changes, with everything else held
fixed. Above the zero line raises the chance; below lowers it.
terms.here:
Shown in the What drives it and What if tabs. For
categories such as region, each level gets its own bar.

terms.name: Two methods must agree
terms.plain:
Each importance method has quirks, so a pattern is
reported only when at least two of the three methods show it. "Rank
agreement" is a correlation between two methods' rankings: 1 means the same
order, 0 means unrelated.
terms.here:
EBM and SHAP agree well (0.58 to 0.76). Drop-one
agrees weakly.

terms.name: Domain
terms.here:
Importance summed by domain shows the balance
shifting from household power (reaching care) to money, distance and
pregnancy intention (completing care).

terms.name: Screening
terms.plain:
Scoring every available column on its own to find
candidates worth reviewing. Each candidate was then checked for timing
(temporality) and leakage.
terms.here:
All 6,648 columns were screened, and 61 new variables
were admitted. Rerunning the screening on development women only admits the
same 61.

terms.name: Duplicates
terms.plain:
The same information present twice under two names
(for example `region` and `v024`). Duplicates split importance between the
copies, so each looks half as important as it is. **Theil's U** measures how
much knowing one variable tells you about another. Checking both directions
separates true copies from variables that merely nest inside each other.
terms.here:
10 of the 95 were copies, leaving 85 distinct.
Removing them changes accuracy by 0.002 AP.

terms.name: Ablation
terms.plain:
Removing or changing one part of an analysis to see
what it was contributing.

terms.name: Add-one test
terms.plain:
Start from the 21-predictor set and add one other
candidate at a time, measuring the gain.
terms.here:
None of the 67 candidates clears the bar alone for
ANC1+ or ANC4+. Six to eight do for ANC8+.

terms.name: Remove-one test
terms.plain:
Start from everything and remove one predictor at a
time.
terms.here:
Almost every removal costs nothing, because
correlated predictors stand in for each other.

terms.name: Forward selection
terms.plain:
Build a set from nothing. At each step, add whichever
predictor helps most. Stop when nothing helps enough.
terms.here:
Run on the 88 candidates for three outcomes, and
again within the 21 alone to find how many of them are needed. Repeated at
the ANC-entry horizon and in the 24-month window.

terms.name: The +0.005 bar
terms.plain:
A variable "pays its way" only if adding it raises AP by
at least 0.005 on average **and** it helps on at least 4 of 5 repeated
splits.
terms.here:
Fixed before any selection result was seen, so the
rule could not be bent to fit the results.

terms.name: Tiers
terms.plain:
- **Tier 1 (core):** the first variables chosen, up to the point where the
  set reaches 90% of what all 88 achieve above prevalence.
- **Tier 2 ("valuable bump"):** further variables that still clear the bar.
terms.here:
Tier 1 is 1 or 2 variables and tier 1+2 is 2 to 8,
depending on the outcome.

terms.name: Selection frequency
terms.plain:
Forward selection is repeated on resampled data. A
variable chosen in most resamples is reliable; one chosen in 20% of them
could easily have been another.

terms.name: Difference-in-differences
terms.plain:
Compare the change over time in one place with the
change over the same time elsewhere. Anything that affected everyone (the
national trend, women forgetting older births) cancels out. What remains is
the change specific to that place.
terms.here:
Tigray, wartime pregnancies against post-war ones,
minus the change in other regions over the same calendar periods. Result: 13
points fewer women with no ANC at all after the war. The survey records ANC
only for births from about mid-2021, so there are no pre-war pregnancies to
compare with.

terms.name: Comparison regions
terms.plain:
The places used as the "elsewhere" in a
difference-in-differences.
terms.here:
Regions without major conflict. Their own change was
near zero (−1.2 to +1.2 points).

terms.name: Simpson's paradox
terms.plain:
A group average can move one way while every subgroup
moves the other way, because the mix of subgroups changed.
terms.here:
Pooled together, the comparison regions seem to fall
5 points between the periods while each region is flat or rising, because
the mix of regions differs between the periods. The estimate therefore
averages the change within each region.

terms.name: Recall bias and survivorship
terms.plain:
- **Recall bias:** women remember older pregnancies less accurately.
- **Survivorship:** women who died, or fled the area, are never
  interviewed.
terms.here:
Both would make the war look *less* damaging than it
was, so the estimates are more likely too small than too large.

terms.name: Regions against their circumstances
terms.plain:
Predict each region's attainment from its women's
wealth, education and household profile, leaving region out. Then compare
with what actually happened. A positive gap means the region does better
than its population would suggest.
terms.here:
Afar is about 15 points above expectation for ANC8+.
Tigray is about 4 below.

fig01_cascade.shows: How far women get on the antenatal care ladder.
fig01_cascade.read:
The left panel has one bar per rung. Taller means more
women reached it. The right panel shows, of the women who reached one rung,
the share who went on (dark) or were lost (grey).
fig01_cascade.takeaway:
78% start and only 19% finish. The biggest loss is between the
fourth and eighth contacts: 63% of women at four go no further.

fig02_regional_cascade.shows: Where each region loses its women.
fig02_regional_cascade.takeaway:
Somali loses two-thirds at the door (red). Central Ethiopia
loses almost half between four and eight (light green). Regions with similar
ANC8+ need opposite programmes.

fig03_continuation_equity.shows:
Among women who **already** reached four contacts, the
share who went on to eight, by wealth, residence and education.
fig03_continuation_equity.read:
Longer bars mean more of these women continued. Because
everyone shown has already attended four times, differences reflect the
cost of returning rather than interest in care.
fig03_continuation_equity.takeaway:
The richest fifth continue 52% of the time and the poorest
fifth 20%.

fig04_leaderboard_anc8plus.shows:
Each of the ten model families' AP in development (grey
dot) and on held-out women (teal dot).
fig04_leaderboard_anc8plus.read:
Further right is better. The grey line is the drop from
development to held-out. Look at how long the lines are compared with how
far apart the models are.
fig04_leaderboard_anc8plus.takeaway:
Every model drops about 0.08 on new women, which is larger
than the differences between models. The choice of algorithm was never what
limited accuracy.

fig05_calibration.shows:
Whether predicted probabilities match reality, on
held-out women.
fig05_calibration.read:
Women are grouped into ten bins by predicted
probability. Each dot plots the bin's average prediction (across) against
the share who actually reached ANC8+ (up). The dashed diagonal is perfect
calibration. Dots below it mean the model over-predicts; dots above it mean
it under-predicts.
fig05_calibration.takeaway:
All models follow the diagonal reasonably well. The zig-zag at
low probabilities is noise from small bins.

fig06_stability.shows:
The 21-predictor set against the full pool (95 columns),
compared on 20 different random splits.
fig06_stability.read:
In the left panel each row is one split: an orange dot
(21 predictors) joined to a teal dot (95). Teal to the right means the 95
won. The right panel collects the 20 gains. The red line at zero is "no
difference".
fig06_stability.takeaway:
The full pool wins on all 20 splits, by +0.031 AP on
average.

fig07_bootstrap.shows:
How certain the held-out comparison between the full-pool
model and the 21-predictor XGBoost is.
fig07_bootstrap.read:
Each histogram shows 2,000 bootstrap re-draws of the
held-out difference. The shaded band is the 95% interval, the dashed line
the estimate, and the red line zero. If the band covers zero, the data
cannot tell the two models apart.
fig07_bootstrap.takeaway:
Both intervals include zero. One held-out set of 1,375 women
is too small to confirm a gain this size, which is why fig06 carries the
claim.

fig08_global_importance.shows:
How much the explainable model relies on each
predictor.
fig08_global_importance.read:
A longer bar means a larger average push on women's
scores, in either direction. The colour gives the domain. Names such as
`v191` are survey codes (v191 is the wealth score; v045c is first
language).
fig08_global_importance.takeaway:
Region, pregnancy intention, first language and the wealth
measures lead. Note that several wealth columns appear separately, so each
looks smaller than wealth really is (see fig24).

fig09_shape_functions.shows:
The explainable model's learned effect of each top
predictor.
fig09_shape_functions.read:
Green bars or curve above zero raise a woman's chance of
ANC8+; red below zero lowers it, on the log-odds scale. For continuous
predictors (such as the wealth score v191), follow the curve from left to
right. For categories, compare the bars.
fig09_shape_functions.takeaway:
"Wanted later" pregnancies and the poorest quintiles pull
scores down most. Addis Ababa and Afar pull them up.

fig10_decision_curve.shows:
Whether acting on the model's predictions beats acting
on everyone or no one.
fig10_decision_curve.read:
Across the bottom is the risk threshold at which you
would act; up the side is net benefit. The model is useful where its line
sits above both "treat all" (grey curve) and "treat none" (flat dotted line
at zero).
fig10_decision_curve.takeaway:
Both models beat the defaults across most thresholds, and the
21-predictor and full-pool models are almost indistinguishable.

fig11_subgroups.shows:
AUROC within each region, wealth group, education level
and residence, for the 21-predictor model (orange) and the full-pool model
(teal).
fig11_subgroups.read:
Further right is better. The dotted red line at 0.5 is a
coin flip. Subgroups are small, so single dots are noisy.
fig11_subgroups.takeaway:
The national AUROC hides regions where the model barely ranks
women at all (Gambella, Central Ethiopia, South West Ethiopia). Within most
regions, the model ranks women less well than it does nationally.

fig14_screening.shows:
The strongest single columns in the whole survey file
(left) and how the screening sorted all columns (right).
fig14_screening.read:
In the left panel, bar length is each column's
univariate AUC. Grey bars were excluded, nearly all because they record
things after or during care (leakage). Teal bars were admitted.
fig14_screening.takeaway:
The strongest columns in the survey are leaks. The strongest
legitimate one is the continuous wealth score (v191, 0.755); the
21-predictor set uses its five-group version.

fig15_preprocessing.shows:
How much AP changes under different ways of preparing
the data (filling gaps, encoding categories).
fig15_preprocessing.read:
Bars to the right of zero improved AP; bars to the left
reduced it. Note the tiny scale: the axis spans less than 0.01.
fig15_preprocessing.takeaway:
Preprocessing barely matters: +0.003 at best, an order of
magnitude less than changing the predictors.

fig16_hyperparameters.shows:
For each tuned setting, the worst AP loss from moving it
away from the tuned value while holding the others fixed.
fig16_hyperparameters.read:
A long bar means the setting matters; a short bar means
the search bought little for it.
fig16_hyperparameters.takeaway:
Most settings matter little. The exceptions are the share of
data and columns each tree sees (XGBoost), whether the EBM may use
interactions, and the regularisation strength C (logistic regression).

fig17_tuning_gain.shows:
How much the whole tuning search improved each model
over its library defaults.
fig17_tuning_gain.read:
A longer bar means tuning helped more. Read it against
the roughly 0.08 drop every model suffers on new women (fig04).
fig17_tuning_gain.takeaway:
Tuning bought 0.00 to 0.04 AP, which is less than the
optimism gap, so it is not evidence that tuned models generalise better.

fig18_ladder_performance.shows: Performance on the three rungs, measured three ways.
fig18_ladder_performance.read:
- **Left:** prevalence, which is what a blind guess scores in AP.
- **Middle:** raw AP, with the dashed box marking that floor. The
  comparable part is the height *above* the box.
- **Right:** AUROC, which does not depend on prevalence (0.5 is chance).
fig18_ladder_performance.takeaway:
Raw AP makes ANC1+ look easiest only because its floor is
highest. AUROC shows the real ordering: reaching care (0.83) is easier to
predict than completing it (0.76).

fig19_ladder_importance.shows:
Each predictor's share of importance at ANC1+ (light),
ANC4+ (mid) and ANC8+ (dark).
fig19_ladder_importance.read:
Follow each row from light to dark dot.
- **Green connecting line:** the predictor matters more as the bar rises
  (completion-limited).
- **Red line:** it matters less (access-limited).
fig19_ladder_importance.takeaway:
Wealth, pregnancy intention and travel time to a health post
grow in importance for completion. Household headship and attitudes to
partner violence matter mostly for reaching care at all.

fig20_domain_rollup.shows:
The same importance, summed into seven domains, across
the three rungs.
fig20_domain_rollup.read:
A line rising from left to right means that domain
matters more for completing care than for reaching it.
fig20_domain_rollup.takeaway:
Agency and household falls (28% → 19%), while socioeconomic
(20% → 26%), reproductive history and access rise.

fig21_regional_gap.shows:
Each region's actual ANC8+ minus what its population
profile predicts.
fig21_regional_gap.read:
A green bar to the right means the region does better
than its circumstances; a red bar to the left means worse. Units are
percentage points.
fig21_regional_gap.takeaway:
Afar (+15), Addis Ababa and Dire Dawa outperform. Tigray,
Gambella and Somali fall short of what their circumstances predict.

fig22_modifiable.shows:
AUROC using everything, using only things a health
service can change (access, services), or using only fixed circumstances.
fig22_modifiable.read:
Compare the bar heights within each rung. The dotted
line at 0.5 is chance.
fig22_modifiable.takeaway:
Fixed circumstances alone nearly match the full model. The
service-related factors carry less predictive signal, though that does not
mean they matter less for policy.

fig23_risk_bands.shows: Women grouped by predicted chance of ANC8+.
fig23_risk_bands.read:
- **Bars (left axis):** the share in each band who actually reached eight
  contacts.
- **Line (right axis):** the share of all women in that band.
fig23_risk_bands.takeaway:
Actual attainment rises steadily with the prediction, so the
ranking works. Most women sit in the low bands.

fig24_redundancy.shows:
Importance before and after counting duplicate columns
as one variable.
fig24_redundancy.read:
The teal part is what one column received; the grey
extension is what its copies added. The note gives the rank now and before.
fig24_redundancy.takeaway:
Travel time to hospital rises from rank 10 to rank 2 once its
copy is counted. Duplicates made important variables look minor.

fig25_set_comparison.shows:
The gain in AP from using the full pool, 85 distinct
variables or 95 columns, instead of the 21-predictor set, on every repeated
split.
fig25_set_comparison.read:
Each dot is one split; the black bar is the mean. The
red line at zero is no gain. Dots all above zero means a consistent gain.
fig25_set_comparison.takeaway:
Small for ANC1+ (+0.008) and ANC4+ (+0.013), larger for ANC8+
(+0.042). The 10 duplicates add nothing (85 ≈ 95).

fig26_add_one.shows:
Each of the 67 pool candidates outside the 21 added
**alone** to the 21, sorted by gain. Top row: all births (the main
analysis); bottom row: the 24-month window (sensitivity).
fig26_add_one.read:
Each thin bar is one candidate. The dashed red line is
the +0.005 bar. Teal bars clear it consistently.
fig26_add_one.takeaway:
For ANC1+ and ANC4+ no candidate clears the bar. For ANC8+, 6
to 8 do. Most candidates sit at zero.

fig27_diminishing_returns.shows:
Development AP as the 67 candidates are stacked onto the
21, best first.
fig27_diminishing_returns.read:
- A curve that rises and then flattens or falls means a few additions carry
  the gain and the rest add nothing or add noise.
- The dashed line is the 21 alone.
- The shaded band shows variation across splits.
fig27_diminishing_returns.takeaway:
On ANC8+ the first handful give most of the gain. Beyond the
peak, extra variables make development scores worse. The held-out test
(fig30) tells a different story for ANC1+ and ANC4+.

fig28_tier_ladders.shows:
Forward selection from nothing: which variable was chosen
at each step, and how much it lifted AP above prevalence.
fig28_tier_ladders.read:
- Rows go top to bottom in the order chosen. Bar length is AP above
  prevalence after adding that variable.
- Dark teal is tier 1, light teal tier 2, grey the first step that failed
  the bar.
- The dashed line is the 21-predictor set and the dotted line is the full
  pool.
fig28_tier_ladders.takeaway:
The household wealth score is chosen first in every run.
Two to eight variables reach roughly the level of the 21.

fig29_selection_frequency.shows:
How often each variable was chosen again when selection
was re-run on ten resamples (ANC8+).
fig29_selection_frequency.read:
Longer means more reliably chosen. Below the dashed 70%
line, a variable's place is not dependable: another similar variable could
take it.
fig29_selection_frequency.takeaway:
Wealth, region and pregnancy intention are reliable. Most
tier-2 places rotate.

fig30_heldout_sets.shows:
The fair test. Each predictor set was fitted on
development women and scored once on held-out women, by outcome (top row: all
births; bottom row: 24-month sensitivity window).
fig30_heldout_sets.read:
Bar height is AP above prevalence (higher is better),
with dark bars for logistic regression and light bars for LightGBM. The
number under each set is how many predictors it uses.
fig30_heldout_sets.takeaway:
The full pool does best for ANC1+ and ANC4+. Compact sets roughly match
the 21 for ANC1+ and ANC8+ and fall short for ANC4+. Most ANC8+ differences
are within the uncertainty.

fig33_drop_within_21.shows:
Each member of the 21-predictor set removed from it in
turn, at each rung, and the AP lost.
fig33_drop_within_21.read:
A green bar to the right means the set needs that
predictor. A grey bar at or left of zero means the set does as well or
better without it. Rows are ordered by ANC8+.
fig33_drop_within_21.takeaway:
Region, pregnancy intention and wealth carry the 21 at every
rung. The number that add nothing grows up the ladder: 8 of 21 for ANC1+, 10
for ANC4+, 14 for ANC8+.

fig34_why21.shows:
How much of the full pool's lift over prevalence a set
reaches, by how many predictors it has: taking the best of the 21 one at a
time (orange), and selecting from the whole pool (teal).
fig34_why21.read:
100% is what the full pool reaches. The dashed line is
all 21 together. An orange point above the dashed line is a smaller subset of
the 21 that does better than all 21. These are development scores, so the
chosen sets are optimistic.
fig34_why21.takeaway:
For ANC8+ the best 7 of the 21 already reach the full pool,
and adding the other 14 lowers the score. For ANC1+ and ANC4+ the curve is
flat: the 21 are about as good as their best subset. The held-out check is
in PREDICTOR_VALUE.md.

fig35_predictor_rung_matrix.shows:
Each predictor's value relative to the 21-predictor set at
ANC1+, ANC4+ and ANC8+, on one comparable scale.
fig35_predictor_rung_matrix.read:
For members of the 21 (marked [21]) the number is the AP
lost when dropped; for the rest, the AP gained when added. Both are shown as
a percentage of each rung's ceiling (full-pool AP minus prevalence). Green is
value, brown is harm. Rows run from most ANC1+-weighted (top) to most
ANC8+-weighted (bottom).
fig35_predictor_rung_matrix.takeaway:
Region and the wealth measures become far more valuable at
ANC8+. Residence, education level and the gap since the previous pregnancy
matter for reaching care and not for completing it.

fig31_tigray_did.shows:
Antenatal care in Tigray for pregnancies during and after
the war (left), and the change beyond what other regions saw over the same
calendar periods (right).
fig31_tigray_did.read:
- **Left:** a red dot for wartime, a teal dot for post-war. The gap is the
  raw change.
- **Right:** the difference-in-differences. A bar right of zero means more
  after the war. The whiskers are the 95% interval; a whisker crossing zero
  means no clear change.
fig31_tigray_did.takeaway:
The war mainly stopped women reaching any care: no-ANC fell
13 points after it. ANC4+ recovered, but ANC8+ did not clearly change.

fig32_regional_gap_cohort.shows:
The regions-against-circumstances gap (fig21), computed
separately for all births (orange) and for births in the last 24 months
(teal).
fig32_regional_gap_cohort.read:
Where the two dots sit close together, the result does
not depend on which window is used.
fig32_regional_gap_cohort.takeaway:
The ranking is stable. Tigray's shortfall is not just an
artefact of older, wartime births.

fig36_horizons.shows:
Held-out AUROC for predictor sets at the ANC-entry
horizon, with and without early ANC, and the same sets fitted before ANC,
all scored on the same 984 women who started ANC.
fig36_horizons.read:
Light bars are without early ANC, dark bars with it,
brown bars the sets fitted on all women before ANC. Longer is better; 0.5 is
chance.
fig36_horizons.takeaway:
Adding early ANC lengthens every bar, most clearly for ANC4+.
Fitting on the entry women instead of all women barely changes anything.

fig37_early_anc.shows:
How much held-out AUROC early ANC adds to each predictor
set, with a 95% interval.
fig37_early_anc.read:
Each dot is the gain from adding early ANC; the line is
its interval. An interval entirely right of the red zero line is a confirmed
gain.
fig37_early_anc.takeaway:
For ANC4+ the gain is confirmed whatever it is added to. For
ANC8+ it is positive but confirmed only when added to the full pool.

fig38_tigray_regions_by_period.shows:
Every region's antenatal care over the same two calendar
periods: pregnancies during the Tigray war window, and pregnancies conceived
after the ceasefire.
fig38_tigray_regions_by_period.read:
A red dot for the wartime period, a teal dot for the
post-war period; a longer grey line is a larger change. Tigray is
highlighted.
fig38_tigray_regions_by_period.takeaway:
Tigray has the largest change of any region in reaching care:
no-ANC falls from 20% to 8% and ANC4+ rises from 46% to 59%, while most
regions move a few points. Its ANC8+ barely moves (10% to 12%).
